context: A B2B SaaS company's authentication system is 4 years old, written in a framework version that is now EOL. A security audit identified 3 medium-severity vulnerabilities tied to the outdated framework's session handling. The audit gives 8 weeks to remediate. The auth system is ~3,000 lines, handles SSO (SAML + OIDC), MFA, API key management, and session tokens. It has 40% test coverage, mostly on the happy paths. Two proposals: (A) incremental refactor — patch the 3 vulnerabilities directly, upgrade the framework version, improve test coverage to 70%, ship incrementally over 6 weeks. (B) full rewrite — rebuild auth on the current framework from scratch with modern patterns, 100% test coverage on security paths, ship as a single cutover in 8 weeks. The team has 3 senior engineers who all know the current system well. No other major projects are competing for their time.
question: Should the team do an incremental refactor (option A) or a full rewrite (option B) of the authentication system?
expert_answer: Incremental refactor (option A). Patch the vulnerabilities first (week 1-2), then upgrade the framework (week 3-5), then improve coverage (week 5-6), shipping each change independently.
expert_reasoning: The rewrite is tempting because the system is old and the team has capacity. But authentication is the highest-risk component in any B2B SaaS — a regression during cutover could lock out all customers or expose session tokens. The rewrite creates a single high-risk deployment at week 8 with zero production validation before then. The incremental approach ships the vulnerability patches in week 2, immediately reducing audit risk, while each subsequent change gets production validation. If the framework upgrade hits an unexpected SSO compatibility issue (SAML implementations are notoriously fragile), the team has 4 weeks of buffer instead of 0. The rewrite also implicitly assumes the team fully understands all the implicit behaviors of the current system — with only 40% test coverage, there are likely undocumented edge cases in session handling, token refresh, and SSO flows that only surface in production. An incremental approach discovers these as it goes, while a rewrite discovers them during a high-stakes cutover.
anti_pattern: Choosing the rewrite because 'we finally have the time and justification.' The security audit creates urgency, not opportunity. Using the audit deadline as leverage to justify a long-desired rewrite conflates two goals: vulnerability remediation (urgent, bounded) and system modernization (important, unbounded). If the rewrite slips past week 8 — and rewrites almost always take longer than estimated — the team has both an unpatched vulnerability AND an incomplete rewrite. The incremental approach decouples these goals: remediate first, modernize on your own timeline afterward.
